# Curriculum vitae: Dr Sorcha Mulqueeney

Head of Coastal Water Quality, Cladach Institute for Coastal Science (CICS), Galway, Ireland
Updated 22 September 2026

## Education

- 2011 PhD in Chemical Oceanography, Corrib University, Galway. Thesis: Dissolved organic matter fluorescence as a tracer of wastewater in macrotidal estuaries.
- 2006 BSc (Hons) Environmental Chemistry, Corrib University.

## Positions

- 2021–present Head of Coastal Water Quality, CICS (team of 9 in Galway; scientific lead for the CICS Shannon Estuary Laboratory since it opened in March 2024).
- 2018–2021 Senior Scientist, CICS.
- 2014–2018 Research Scientist, CICS.
- 2012–2014 Marie Curie Intra-European Fellow, Laboratoire de Chimie des Eaux Littorales (LCEL), Université de Rochefort-Charente, France (FP7 project ESTUFLUOR).
- 2011–2012 Postdoctoral researcher, Corrib University.

## Research funding

|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2021–2024 | BAYPROXY | EPA Research Programme 2021–2030, grant 2021-W-MS-47 | PI | EUR 398,000 |

Unfunded application: OUTFALERT, Horizon Europe Research and Innovation Action, coordinator. Submitted 16 September 2025, EUR 3,000,000 requested. Total score 10.50/15, all thresholds passed, not retained for funding (evaluation summary report received 10 February 2026).

## Coordination experience

Coordinated BAYPROXY, a single-beneficiary national grant with two subcontracted analyses. Has not coordinated a multi-beneficiary EU project. CICS has not coordinated a Horizon 2020 or Horizon Europe project.

## Supervision

Three PhD students co-supervised with Corrib University (two completed, 2022 and 2025; one ongoing). Four postdoctoral researchers supervised at CICS.

## Activities since February 2026

- Co-author, with URC, of the two-estuary calibration protocol OUTFALERT-CAL-2E v1.0 (approved 30 June 2026).
- Corresponding author of a manuscript on bootstrap propagation of proxy-assay error into warning outcomes, submitted 20 August 2026, under review.
- Signed the CICS letter of commitment (9 September 2026) and the consortium memorandum of understanding (18 September 2026).

## Service

Reviewer for the EPA Research Programme (2022–2025). Editorial board member, Estuarine Water Quality Letters, since 2023.

## Publications

22 peer-reviewed articles, 14 as first or last author. Selected items in publications.md.

# OUTFALERT consortium: partners, team and resources

Status at 30 September 2026

## Participation

Three legal entities in three countries have signed letters of commitment to take part in a joint Horizon Europe application continuing the OUTFALERT work: CICS (9 September 2026), URC (11 September 2026) and WISW (16 September 2026). A consortium memorandum of understanding covering roles, background intellectual property and data access was signed by all three on 18 September 2026.

| No. | Entity | Country | Legal status | Main expertise |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Cladach Institute for Coastal Science (CICS), Galway | Ireland | Independent research organisation; company limited by guarantee (2009); registered charity | Coastal water quality, hydrodynamic modelling, microbiology |
| 2 | Université de Rochefort-Charente (URC), Laboratoire de Chimie des Eaux Littorales (LCEL) | France | Public university | Environmental chemistry, organic-matter fluorescence |
| 3 | Weser-Institut für Stadt- und Wasserplanung (WISW) e.V., Bremen | Germany | Non-profit registered association | Urban water and stormwater planning |

The three entities have no shared ownership, control or management.

### CICS Shannon Estuary Laboratory

The Shannon Estuary Laboratory in Foynes, Co. Limerick, opened in March 2024, is a department of CICS. It has no separate legal personality, company registration or PIC; its contracts, accounts and legal signatory are those of CICS. Head: Dr Eoin Fennessy-Ward; 5 staff. In April–May 2026 it ran the proxy assay on 20 split samples from Galway; its exceedance classification agreed with the Galway laboratory in 18 of 20 samples. It has collected no samples from the Shannon estuary.

## Team and facilities

### CICS (52 staff; income EUR 4.3 million in 2025)

- Dr Sorcha Mulqueeney: coordinator; chemical oceanography (see CV).
- Dr Eoin Fennessy-Ward: head of the Shannon Estuary Laboratory; PhD in environmental microbiology (2015); developed the glucuronidase assay protocol.
- Dr Méabh Costigan-Reidy: hydrodynamic modeller; built the TELEMAC-2D model of inner Galway Bay.
- Dr Ruairí Tobin-Hayes: statistician; author of the outfalert-uq code; covers data management at 0.2 FTE. CICS has no dedicated data steward.
- Two laboratory technicians (Galway).

Facilities: microbiology laboratory accredited to ISO/IEC 17025 for ISO 9308-3; three field fluorometers; glucuronidase assay set-ups in Galway and Foynes; 7-m survey boat; 512-core compute cluster.

EU track record: work-package lead in ESTUWARD-PB19 (Interreg Atlantic Area 2014–2020; 2019–2022). CICS has not coordinated a Horizon 2020 or Horizon Europe project.

### URC, LCEL

- Prof. Clémence Arbogast-Riou: environmental chemistry; excitation–emission matrix (EEM) fluorescence and PARAFAC; host of Dr Mulqueeney's 2012–2014 fellowship.
- Dr Bastien Morvillier: environmental microbiology; runs culture methods.
- One engineer; one PhD student (thesis on organic-matter fluorescence in the Charente, started October 2025).

Facilities: EEM spectrofluorometer; culture laboratory; small boat at Rochefort. Culture methods run under the university quality system; the laboratory is not accredited for ISO 9308-3. EU track record: partner in two Horizon 2020 projects (2016–2020 and 2018–2022).

### WISW (31 staff)

- Dr.-Ing. Henrike Wolfsteller: urban water planning; overflow-reduction programmes and stormwater master plans.
- Jonas Kettler, M.Sc.: planning economics; drafted the decision-cost table (July 2026).
- Dr. Lene Brakhage: participatory planning; municipal workshops.

Experience: stormwater master plans and overflow-reduction studies for three municipalities in Lower Saxony and Bremen (2016–2024); partner in one Interreg North Sea Region project. WISW has no water-quality monitoring or laboratory capacity and had no experience with bathing-water warning systems before joining OUTFALERT in 2025.

## Users and municipalities

- The Galway local authority provided beach-attendance counter data to BAYPROXY (2022–2024), and its bathing-water officer attended two BAYPROXY meetings in 2023. It has not reviewed the decision-cost table and has not given a letter of support.
- WISW held exploratory calls with the drainage departments of two municipalities in Lower Saxony (12 May and 9 June 2026) about overflow notification for urban watercourses. Both asked to be kept informed; neither has committed staff, data or a letter.
- No municipality, water utility or bathing-water authority is a member of the consortium.
- The consortium holds no monitoring data from inland urban watercourses or river bathing sites; all its contamination data come from estuaries and coastal bathing waters.

## Collaboration history

CICS and URC have worked together since 2012 (fellowship; two joint publications). CICS and WISW have worked together since February 2025 (OUTFALERT preparation; decision-cost table 2026).

# Final report: BAYPROXY (2021–2024)

**Rapid faecal-contamination proxies and overflow-driven exceedance forecasting for Galway Bay bathing waters**

Funded by the EPA Research Programme 2021–2030, grant 2021-W-MS-47, EUR 398,000, 1 April 2021 to 30 September 2024 (including a six-month no-cost extension). Lead organisation: Cladach Institute for Coastal Science (CICS), Galway. Principal investigator: Dr Sorcha Mulqueeney. Report submitted 20 December 2024.

## 1. Objectives

1. Calibrate a rapid proxy for faecal contamination, combining tryptophan-like fluorescence (TLF) and β-D-glucuronidase (GLUC) activity, against culture-based *E. coli* in the Corrib estuary and inner Galway Bay.
2. Relate storm-overflow spills, rainfall and tide to exceedances at four designated bathing waters (B1–B4).
3. Describe how beach users receive water-quality information.

## 2. Methods

- **Stations.** Nine stations from the lower Corrib estuary to the bathing waters: five estuarine and transitional stations (E1–E5) and B1–B4. Sampling in the 2021, 2022 and 2023 bathing seasons (1 June to 15 September).
- **Routine sampling.** 22 fortnightly visits were scheduled (7, 8 and 7 per season) and 21 completed; one visit in July 2022 was cancelled for weather. Each visit covered four of the nine stations on a fixed rotation, so that every station was sampled at least every six weeks: 84 samples.
- **Event sampling.** Within 48 h of rainfall above 8 mm in 24 h, samples were taken at B1–B4 and at the two stations nearest the outfalls (E4, E5): 11 events (3, 4 and 4 per season), 66 samples.
- **Exclusions.** 8 of the 150 samples (3 routine, 5 event) were excluded before analysis: 5 because culture started more than 24 h after collection, 3 because the field fluorometer failed its daily drift check. The analysed set is 142 paired samples (81 routine, 61 event), each with proxy and culture from the same bottle; salinity 4–34.
- **Reference method.** *E. coli* by ISO 9308-3 (miniaturised MPN) in the CICS microbiology laboratory, accredited to ISO/IEC 17025 for this method. Exceedance: a single sample above 500 MPN/100 mL.
- **Proxy.** TLF (peak T) read with a field fluorometer; GLUC activity from a 2-hour fluorogenic assay. A logistic classifier on TLF, GLUC and salinity was fitted with leave-one-season-out cross-validation; the cut-off maximised the Youden index. Sensitivity and specificity are computed from out-of-fold predictions. Uncertainty from 2,000 bootstrap resamples stratified by season.
- **Overflows and exceedance model.** Spill telemetry for four storm overflows (2019–2023, 187 spill events) supplied by the national water utility under a data-sharing agreement that prohibits redistribution. Hourly rainfall from Met Éireann gauges. A TELEMAC-2D model of inner Galway Bay (unstructured mesh, 40–250 m) gave outfall-to-beach travel times by particle tracking. A logistic model of exceedance at B1–B4 used observed 24-h rainfall to 09:00 on the sample day, observed spill duration in the preceding 24 h, tidal state at sampling and onshore wind. It was evaluated against regulatory and investigative samples from 2019–2023 (486 sample-days) by leave-one-year-out cross-validation: probabilities for each year come from a model fitted to the other four years. All predictors are observations available at sampling time, so the evaluation is a retrospective hindcast at zero lead time; no rainfall forecasts were used.
- **Survey.** Intercept survey of 612 beach users at B1–B4, July–August 2023, in English only.

## 3. Results

- **Exceedances.** 25 of 142 paired samples (17.6%) exceeded 500 MPN/100 mL: 21 of the 61 event samples and 4 of the 81 routine samples.
- **Proxy performance.** Sensitivity **0.76** (19 of 25; bootstrap 95% CI 0.55–0.90); specificity **0.88** (103 of 117; 95% CI 0.81–0.93). Log proxy score correlated with log *E. coli* (r = 0.71, n = 142). Four of the six false negatives occurred at salinity above 30, where the GLUC signal is diluted.
- **Travel time.** Median outfall-to-beach travel time 6.5 h (interquartile range 3.5–11.0 h).
- **Hindcast skill.** Out-of-fold area under the ROC curve **0.81** (95% CI 0.74–0.87, bootstrap over sample-days) over 486 sample-days, of which 38 were exceedances. With warnings issued at a predicted probability of 0.5, 20 of the 38 exceedances were warned (hit rate 0.53) and 8 of 28 warnings were false alarms (false alarm ratio 0.29).
- **Beach users.** 23% of respondents (141 of 612) relied only on on-site signs for water-quality information; 31% (190 of 612) swam outside the bathing season, when no regulatory sampling takes place; 57% (349 of 612) had entered the water on the day of interview.
- **Data.** The paired proxy–culture dataset (142 samples, with station metadata) was deposited in Zenodo under CC BY 4.0 in October 2024. Spill telemetry and survey microdata were not deposited: the first is covered by the data-sharing agreement, the second by a consent form that allows release of aggregated tables only.

## 4. Limitations

- All calibration samples come from one estuary. Classifier coefficients may depend on salinity regime, organic-matter background and effluent composition; transfer to other estuaries was not tested.
- With 25 exceedances, the sensitivity estimate is imprecise.
- The proxy targets faecal indicator bacteria; no pathogens (for example norovirus) were measured.
- Skill at forecast lead times was not tested. The AUC refers to a zero-lead hindcast with observed rainfall and observed spills; a day-ahead forecast would depend on rainfall forecasts and predicted spills.
- The 0.5 warning cut-off was chosen for illustration; no bathing-water manager was involved in setting it.
- The survey was a convenience sample in English and under-represents non-English speakers and early-morning and winter swimmers.

## 5. Outputs

Two peer-reviewed articles (2023, 2024), one MSc thesis, five conference presentations, the open paired dataset, and an internal prototype run daily at CICS during the 2024 bathing season that gave same-day exceedance probabilities from observed rainfall and telemetry (not issued to the public; its outputs were not systematically compared with samples).

# OUTFALERT: Horizon Europe RIA proposal, abridged copy

**Outfall-to-beach alerts: storm-contamination warnings for coastal bathing waters fed by urban outfalls**

| | |
|---|---|
| Submitted | 16 September 2025 |
| Call | Horizon Europe Cluster 6, 2025 work programme, Zero Pollution destination; single-stage RIA topic |
| Proposal number | 101219884 |
| Duration | 36 months |
| Requested EU contribution | EUR 3,000,000 |
| Coordinator | Cladach Institute for Coastal Science (CICS), Ireland |
| Beneficiaries | Université de Rochefort-Charente (URC), France; Weser-Institut für Stadt- und Wasserplanung (WISW) e.V., Germany |

Abridged by the coordinator in October 2025 from Part B as submitted. Sentences in quotation marks are unchanged; the rest is shortened.

## 1. Excellence

### 1.1 Objectives

- **O1.** Transfer a rapid faecal-contamination proxy, calibrated in Galway Bay, to a second European estuary and quantify its performance there.
- **O2.** Build a 24–48 h warning chain from rainfall nowcasts and overflow telemetry to bathing sites, with a skill target of AUC ≥ 0.80 at each site.
- **O3.** Define warning thresholds and integrate warnings into municipal stormwater and beach-management planning.
- **O4.** Release open data and replicable tools for other outfall-affected coastal sites.

### 1.2 Starting point: BAYPROXY results

BAYPROXY (EPA Research Programme, 2021–2024) produced 142 paired proxy–culture samples from the Corrib estuary and inner Galway Bay. The combined fluorescence–enzymatic proxy detected exceedance of 500 MPN/100 mL with sensitivity 0.76 (95% CI 0.55–0.90) and specificity 0.88. An exceedance model driven by rainfall and spill telemetry reached AUC 0.81 on 486 sample-days at four bathing waters. Median outfall-to-beach travel time was 6.5 h, which leaves time for same-day warnings. A survey of 612 beach users showed that 23% relied only on on-site signs.

### 1.3 Methodology

**Proxy transfer (WP2, lead URC).** “The classifier coefficients calibrated in BAYPROXY will be applied unchanged at three bathing sites at the mouth of the Charente estuary. URC will collect 30 verification samples in year 2 to confirm performance.” URC characterises the organic-matter background at all Charente stations by EEM fluorescence and PARAFAC and analyses 24 outfall effluent samples to compare source signatures with Galway.

**Warning chain (WP3, lead CICS).** Inputs: 1-km radar rainfall nowcasts licensed from Skerrymet Radar Analytics Ltd; overflow telemetry from the Irish national water utility; overflow logs from the wastewater operator at the Charente mouth. The BAYPROXY exceedance model is refitted with nowcast inputs and combined with TELEMAC-2D travel times for Galway and a new TELEMAC-2D set-up for the Charente mouth (month 12). Output: exceedance probabilities 24 h and 48 h ahead, produced daily at 06:00 for B1–B4 and the three Charente sites and run in shadow mode (not public) during two bathing seasons. “A warning is issued when the predicted probability of exceedance is 0.5 or higher.”

**Planning integration (WP4, lead WISW).** WISW maps the warning chain onto stormwater master plans and overflow-reduction programmes, using desk studies of two North Sea municipalities and the Galway case, and writes a planning guidance note for municipalities (month 33). Three user workshops: Galway, Rochefort, Bremen.

**Open science.** Preregistration of the Charente verification analysis; code on a public repository under Apache 2.0; FAIR data management plan in month 6.

## 2. Impact

### 2.1 Expected outcomes and impacts

“OUTFALERT warnings would avoid about 3,400 bather exposures per season at the four Galway Bay pilot beaches.” The figure combined hindcast exceedance days (2019–2023) with mean daily attendance. Charente benefits were not quantified. Target groups: local authorities, wastewater operators and bathers, including year-round swimmers. Replication at 20 European bathing sites by 2030 through the guidance note and open tools. Contribution to the Bathing Water Directive and the Zero Pollution Action Plan.

### 2.2 Dissemination, exploitation and communication

“All project data, including overflow telemetry, radar inputs and survey data, will be published under CC BY 4.0 on Zenodo by month 36.” The same section states: “Overflow telemetry is provided under data-sharing agreements with the operators, and radar nowcasts are licensed from a commercial provider.” Other measures: open-source warning software, a policy brief, three peer-reviewed articles and the three workshops.

## 3. Implementation

### 3.1 Work plan and effort (person-months)

| WP | Title | Lead | CICS | URC | WISW | Total |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| WP1 | Management | CICS | 14 | 2 | 2 | 18 |
| WP2 | Proxy transfer and source chemistry | URC | 12 | 78 | 0 | 90 |
| WP3 | Warning chain and hindcast | CICS | 108 | 10 | 4 | 122 |
| WP4 | Thresholds and planning integration | WISW | 12 | 6 | 70 | 88 |
| WP5 | Dissemination and open data | CICS | 22 | 6 | 8 | 36 |
| Total | | | 168 | 102 | 84 | 354 |

### 3.2 Requested EU contribution

| Beneficiary | EUR |
|---|---|
| CICS | 1,412,500 |
| URC | 868,750 |
| WISW | 718,750 |
| Total | 3,000,000 |

### 3.3 Risks

| Risk | Mitigation |
|---|---|
| Fewer exceedance events than expected | Event-triggered sampling after heavy rainfall |
| Delayed access to overflow telemetry | Use 2019–2023 historical records for model development |
| Low workshop participation | Invitations through WISW's municipal network |

### 3.4 Consortium

Three beneficiaries in three countries. No municipality or bathing-water authority is a beneficiary; users are engaged through workshops. No letters of support were attached.

# Evaluation Summary Report

| | |
|---|---|
| Programme | Horizon Europe, Cluster 6 |
| Call | HORIZON-CL6-2025 (single-stage) |
| Type of action | HORIZON-RIA Research and Innovation Actions |
| Proposal number | 101219884 |
| Acronym | OUTFALERT |
| Title | Outfall-to-beach alerts: storm-contamination warnings for coastal bathing waters fed by urban outfalls |
| Date of notification | 10 February 2026 |

**Total score: 10.50** (threshold 10.00)

| Criterion | Score | Threshold |
|---|---|---|
| 1. Excellence | 3.50 | 3.00 |
| 2. Impact | 3.00 | 3.00 |
| 3. Quality and efficiency of the implementation | 4.00 | 3.00 |

The proposal passed all thresholds. It was ranked below the budget available for the topic and is not proposed for funding.

## Criterion 1: Excellence (score 3.50)

The objectives are clear, pertinent to the topic and include a measurable skill target. The preliminary data from 142 paired samples are credible, and combining fluorescence and enzymatic signals with hydrodynamic travel times is a sound approach that goes beyond current practice for overflow-affected beaches. Chemistry, oceanography and planning are integrated.

The following shortcomings are identified:

- The calibration of the faecal-contamination proxy rests entirely on samples from one estuary (Corrib). The proposal applies the same coefficients unchanged at the Charente sites and plans only 30 verification samples in year 2. Given the known dependence of fluorescence and enzymatic signals on salinity and organic-matter background, transferability is assumed rather than tested, and the verification set is too small to estimate performance with useful precision.
- Warning thresholds are set at a fixed predicted probability of 0.5 without justification. The proposal does not identify who would act on a warning, what action would follow, or how the consequences of false alarms and missed events would determine the threshold. A decision rule for users is lacking.
- Open science practices are described in general terms. Preregistration of the verification analysis is a positive element, but beyond a data management plan announced for month 6 the proposal gives no concrete approach to managing and sharing research outputs.

## Criterion 2: Impact (score 3.00)

The pathways to impact are relevant to the implementation of the Bathing Water Directive. Target groups (local authorities, wastewater operators, bathers) are identified, and communication measures are adequate.

The following shortcomings are identified:

- The headline impact of about 3,400 avoided bather exposures per season is given as a single value. It does not account for proxy misclassification, uncertainty in travel times or in beach attendance, and no range is given. The scale and significance of the expected impacts are therefore not credibly substantiated.
- The dissemination plan commits to publishing all project data, including overflow telemetry, radar inputs and survey data, under an open licence, while the same section states that these data are held under data-sharing agreements and commercial licences. The open-data commitment is not credible as written, and the data management approach is insufficiently thought through.
- The replication target of 20 sites by 2030 is not substantiated, and no end-user organisation has committed to the project.

## Criterion 3: Quality and efficiency of the implementation (score 4.00)

The work plan is coherent, with clear lead responsibilities. The partners are complementary, and CICS and URC have collaborated before. Resources are appropriate overall.

The following shortcomings are identified:

- The risk table is thin. Event-triggered sampling is proposed against a shortage of exceedance events, but the Charente verification relies on 30 samples collected in a single season; if heavy-rainfall events are few in that season, the proposal foresees no contingency such as an additional season, additional sites or a revised analysis.
- The coordinator has limited experience in managing multi-beneficiary EU projects, although the management structure is adequate.

# OUTFALERT consortium: technical update since the evaluation summary report

Prepared by CICS (S. Mulqueeney) for the consortium partners. Version of 30 September 2026. Covers February to September 2026; all work funded from the partners' own resources.

## 1. Second-estuary calibration (ESR, Excellence, first shortcoming)

**Protocol.** OUTFALERT-CAL-2E v1.0 was approved by CICS and URC on 30 June 2026. It replaces the 2025 design (Corrib coefficients applied unchanged in the Charente, plus 30 verification samples in one season) with:

- independent calibration in each estuary (Corrib, Ireland; Charente, France), coefficients fitted separately and then cross-tested (fit in one estuary, test in the other);
- event-triggered sampling after rainfall above 8 mm in 24 h or a recorded overflow spill, spread over two bathing seasons per estuary;
- a target of 115 paired samples per estuary, at least 40 of them exceedances, giving an expected half-width of about 0.13 for the 95% CI of sensitivity. In BAYPROXY, 21 of 61 event samples (34%) exceeded; at that rate about 116 event samples yield 40 exceedances, so the target assumes that almost all samples are taken during events;
- exchange of 10% of samples as split samples between the CICS and URC culture laboratories;
- a transfer rule (protocol section 7): coefficients from one estuary are accepted for the other only if, in the receiving estuary, the lower 95% bound for sensitivity is at least 0.60 and specificity is at least 0.80; otherwise that estuary keeps site-specific coefficients and the transfer is reported as failed.

The protocol has no rule for an estuary that yields fewer than 40 exceedances. Funding for the full campaign has not been secured. Apart from the pilot below, no sampling under the protocol has started.

**Charente pilot.** URC collected 6 paired samples at three stations at the mouth of the Charente between 22 July and 28 August 2026 (salinity 12–31). By culture, 1 sample exceeded 500 MPN/100 mL. The classifier with BAYPROXY coefficients flagged that sample and gave one false positive; 5 of 6 samples were classified correctly. With one exceedance, these data give no usable estimate of sensitivity or specificity in the Charente. The only sensitivity estimate remains the Corrib value of 0.76 (bootstrap 95% CI 0.55–0.90), which is preliminary. Cross-estuary validation has not been done.

**Shannon Estuary Laboratory.** The CICS Shannon Estuary Laboratory ran the proxy assay on 20 split samples from Galway in April–May 2026; its exceedance classification agreed with the Galway laboratory in 18 of 20 samples. No samples from the Shannon estuary have been collected.

## 2. Decision-cost table (ESR, Excellence, second shortcoming)

WISW drafted a decision-cost table (draft v0.2, 31 July 2026; authors J. Kettler and H. Wolfsteller) to replace the fixed 0.5 warning probability with a cost-based rule. Costs are per beach-day and bathing water.

| Outcome | Bears the cost | Cost items | Range (EUR) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Warning, exceedance occurs | Local authority; bathers | Signage and staff (avoided illness not counted) | 1,900–4,600 |
| Warning, no exceedance (false alarm) | Local authority; local businesses | Signage and staff; lost trade; loss of trust (not priced) | 1,900–4,600 |
| No warning, exceedance (miss) | Bathers; health system; local authority | Gastrointestinal illness at assumed attack rates; lost workdays; complaint handling | 14,000–38,000 |
| No warning, no exceedance | none | none | 0 |

Under a cost–loss rule (warn when the predicted probability exceeds the ratio of action cost to avoidable loss), the table implies thresholds between 0.05 and 0.33, with a central value of 0.14 (EUR 3,000 / EUR 22,000), against the fixed 0.5 of the 2025 application. Applied to the out-of-fold BAYPROXY hindcast probabilities (486 sample-days, 38 exceedances), a threshold of 0.14 would have warned 32 of the 38 exceedances (hit rate 0.84) with 61 warnings in total, 29 of them false alarms (false alarm ratio 0.48).

The table is a draft. Cost ranges come from published illness-cost studies and CICS and URC estimates of signage and staff costs. No local authority, bathing-water manager or wastewater operator has reviewed it; no organisation has agreed to own or apply a decision rule; its usefulness to decision-makers has not been tested. Responsibility for bathing-water management and public information lies with local authorities in Ireland (Bathing Water Quality Regulations 2008) and with the commune in France; in Germany it is set by Land bathing-water ordinances.

## 3. Uncertainty in impact estimates (ESR, Impact, first shortcoming)

**Quantity.** The 2025 figure of 3,400 counted, for each 2019–2023 hindcast exceedance day at B1–B4, the mean daily attendance as exposures. It assumed that (i) every attendee enters the water, (ii) a warning issued at a predicted probability of 0.5 or higher, posted on site and online for the whole beach-day, reaches every attendee, (iii) every warned person stays out of the water, and (iv) the proxy classifies perfectly. It is a modelled count of potentially avoidable exposures, not an observed reduction.

**Code.** outfalert-uq v0.3 (Python, 15 June 2026; author Dr R. Tobin-Hayes) removes assumption (iv) and propagates, over 10,000 bootstrap replicates: (a) proxy misclassification, by resampling the 142 BAYPROXY paired samples and reclassifying proxy-flagged exceedance days; (b) outfall-to-beach travel time, from a 50-member TELEMAC-2D ensemble; (c) beach attendance, from counter data for 2022–2024 with a ±20% recording error.

**Results.** Under assumptions (i)–(iii) and the 0.5 threshold: median 2,580 potentially avoidable exposures per season at B1–B4 (95% interval 1,610–3,390), an upper bound. In a sensitivity run that replaces attendance by water entrants (57%, 349 of 612 survey respondents, resampled binomially) and assumes that half of warned bathers stay out of the water (an assumed value; no compliance data exist for Galway Bay): median 740 (95% interval 450–990).

**Not included.** Warning reach and behavioural response (fixed by assumption); error of forecasts at positive lead times (section 5); transfer to other estuaries, which cannot be included until second-estuary data exist; out-of-season swimming; illness given exposure. The intervals cover the Corrib only. A manuscript was submitted on 20 August 2026 and is under review. The code is in the CICS internal repository and is not public.

## 4. Data inventory (ESR, Impact, second shortcoming)

Data inventory v1.0 (25 September 2026), compiled by R. Tobin-Hayes with partner input, was updated to v1.1 on 29 September 2026 to add the 2026 observations (U1, U2). It lists 14 data assets: restricted raw (5), unrestricted raw not yet deposited (2), shareable derived (5) and already open (2).

| ID | Asset | Holder | Class | Licence or condition |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| R1 | Overflow spill telemetry, 4 Galway outfalls | National water utility | Restricted raw | Data-sharing agreement to 31 December 2027; no redistribution of raw or event-level records |
| R2 | 1-km radar rainfall nowcasts | Skerrymet Radar Analytics Ltd | Restricted raw | Commercial licence, internal use only |
| R3 | Overflow logs, Charente | Local wastewater operator | Restricted raw | Convention with URC; no redistribution |
| R4 | BAYPROXY survey microdata (612 respondents) | CICS | Restricted raw | Consent covers aggregated release only |
| R5 | Beach-attendance counter data | Galway local authority | Restricted raw | Permission for research use only |
| U1 | Charente pilot paired proxy–culture records (6 samples, July–August 2026) | URC | Unrestricted raw, not deposited | No third-party restriction; release requires URC approval |
| U2 | Galway–Shannon split-sample assay results (20 samples, April–May 2026) | CICS | Unrestricted raw, not deposited | No third-party restriction |

# Final report: BAYPROXY (2021–2024)

**Rapid faecal-contamination proxies and overflow-driven exceedance forecasting for Galway Bay bathing waters**

Funded by the EPA Research Programme 2021–2030, grant 2021-W-MS-47, EUR 398,000, 1 April 2021 to 30 September 2024 (including a six-month no-cost extension). Lead organisation: Cladach Institute for Coastal Science (CICS), Galway. Principal investigator: Dr Sorcha Mulqueeney. Report submitted 20 December 2024.

## 1. Objectives

1. Calibrate a rapid proxy for faecal contamination, combining tryptophan-like fluorescence (TLF) and β-D-glucuronidase (GLUC) activity, against culture-based *E. coli* in the Corrib estuary and inner Galway Bay.
2. Relate storm-overflow spills, rainfall and tide to exceedances at four designated bathing waters (B1–B4).
3. Describe how beach users receive water-quality information.

## 2. Methods

- **Sampling.** Nine stations from the lower Corrib estuary to B1–B4 in the 2021, 2022 and 2023 bathing seasons (1 June to 15 September): routine fortnightly sampling plus event sampling within 48 h of rainfall above 8 mm in 24 h. 142 paired samples (proxy and culture from the same bottle); salinity 4–34.
- **Reference method.** *E. coli* by ISO 9308-3 (miniaturised MPN) in the CICS microbiology laboratory, accredited to ISO/IEC 17025 for this method. Exceedance: a single sample above 500 MPN/100 mL.
- **Proxy.** TLF (peak T) read with a field fluorometer; GLUC activity from a 2-hour fluorogenic assay. A logistic classifier on TLF, GLUC and salinity was fitted with leave-one-season-out cross-validation; the cut-off maximised the Youden index. Uncertainty from 2,000 bootstrap resamples stratified by season.
- **Overflows and forecast model.** Spill telemetry for four storm overflows (2019–2023, 187 spill events) supplied by the national water utility under a data-sharing agreement that prohibits redistribution. Hourly rainfall from Met Éireann gauges. A TELEMAC-2D model of inner Galway Bay (unstructured mesh, 40–250 m) gave outfall-to-beach travel times by particle tracking. A logistic model of exceedance at B1–B4 used 24-h rainfall, spill duration, tidal state and onshore wind, and was evaluated against regulatory and investigative samples from 2019–2023 (486 sample-days).
- **Survey.** Intercept survey of 612 beach users at B1–B4, July–August 2023, in English only.

## 3. Results

- **Exceedances.** 25 of 142 paired samples (17.6%) exceeded 500 MPN/100 mL; 21 of the 25 were event samples.
- **Proxy performance.** Sensitivity **0.76** (19 of 25; bootstrap 95% CI 0.55–0.90); specificity **0.88** (103 of 117; 95% CI 0.81–0.93). Log proxy score correlated with log *E. coli* (r = 0.71, n = 142). Four of the six false negatives occurred at salinity above 30, where the GLUC signal is diluted.
- **Travel time.** Median outfall-to-beach travel time 6.5 h (interquartile range 3.5–11.0 h).
- **Forecast skill.** Area under the ROC curve **0.81** (95% CI 0.74–0.87) over 486 sample-days, of which 38 were exceedances. With warnings issued at a predicted probability of 0.5, 20 of the 38 exceedances were warned (hit rate 0.53) and 8 of 28 warnings were false alarms (false alarm ratio 0.29).
- **Beach users.** 23% of respondents (141 of 612) relied only on on-site signs for water-quality information; 31% (190 of 612) swam outside the bathing season, when no regulatory sampling takes place.
- **Data.** The paired proxy–culture dataset (142 samples, with station metadata) was deposited in Zenodo under CC BY 4.0 in October 2024. Spill telemetry and survey microdata were not deposited: the first is covered by the data-sharing agreement, the second by a consent form that allows release of aggregated tables only.

## 4. Limitations

- All calibration samples come from one estuary. Classifier coefficients may depend on salinity regime, organic-matter background and effluent composition; transfer to other estuaries was not tested.
- With 25 exceedances, the sensitivity estimate is imprecise.
- The proxy targets faecal indicator bacteria; no pathogens (for example norovirus) were measured.
- The 0.5 warning cut-off was chosen for illustration; no bathing-water manager was involved in setting it.
- The survey was a convenience sample in English and under-represents non-English speakers and early-morning and winter swimmers.

## 5. Outputs

Two peer-reviewed articles (2023, 2024), one MSc thesis, five conference presentations, the open paired dataset, and an internal forecast prototype run daily at CICS during the 2024 bathing season (not issued to the public).

The proposal passed all thresholds. It was ranked below the budget available for the topic and is not proposed for funding.

## Criterion 1: Excellence (score 3.50)

The objectives are clear, pertinent to the topic and include a measurable skill target. The preliminary data from 142 paired samples are credible, and combining fluorescence and enzymatic signals with hydrodynamic travel times is a sound approach that goes beyond current practice for overflow-affected beaches. Chemistry, oceanography and planning are integrated.

The following shortcomings are identified:

- The calibration of the pathogen proxy rests entirely on samples from one estuary (Corrib). The proposal applies the same coefficients unchanged at the Charente sites and plans only 30 verification samples in year 2. Given the known dependence of fluorescence and enzymatic signals on salinity and organic-matter background, transferability is assumed rather than tested, and the verification set is too small to estimate performance with useful precision.
- Warning thresholds are set at a fixed predicted probability of 0.5 without justification. The proposal does not identify who would act on a warning, what action would follow, or how the consequences of false alarms and missed events would determine the threshold. A decision rule for users is lacking.
- Open science practices are described in general terms, although preregistration of the verification analysis is a positive element.

## Criterion 2: Impact (score 3.00)

The pathways to impact are relevant to the implementation of the Bathing Water Directive. Target groups (local authorities, wastewater operators, bathers) are identified, and communication measures are adequate.

The following shortcomings are identified:

- The headline impact of about 3,400 avoided bather exposures per season is given as a single value. It does not account for proxy misclassification, uncertainty in travel times or in beach attendance, and no range is given. The scale and significance of the expected impacts are therefore not credibly substantiated.
- The dissemination plan commits to publishing all project data, including overflow telemetry, radar inputs and survey data, under an open licence, while the same section states that these data are held under data-sharing agreements and commercial licences. The open-data commitment is not credible as written, and the data management approach is insufficiently thought through.
- The replication target of 20 sites by 2030 is not substantiated, and no end-user organisation has committed to the project.

## Criterion 3: Quality and efficiency of the implementation (score 4.00)

The work plan is coherent, with clear lead responsibilities. The partners are complementary, and CICS and URC have collaborated before. Resources are appropriate overall.

The following shortcomings are identified:

- The risk table is thin; there is no mitigation if too few exceedance events occur at the Charente sites.
- The coordinator has limited experience in managing multi-beneficiary EU projects, although the management structure is adequate.

# OUTFALERT consortium: technical update since the evaluation summary report

Prepared by CICS (S. Mulqueeney) for the consortium partners. Version of 30 September 2026. Covers February to September 2026; all work funded from the partners' own resources.

## 1. Second-estuary calibration (ESR, Excellence, first shortcoming)

**Protocol.** OUTFALERT-CAL-2E v1.0 was approved by CICS and URC on 30 June 2026. It replaces the 2025 design (Corrib coefficients applied unchanged in the Charente, plus 30 verification samples) with:

- independent calibration in each estuary (Corrib, Ireland; Charente, France), coefficients fitted separately and then cross-tested (fit in one estuary, test in the other);
- event-triggered sampling (rainfall above 8 mm in 24 h or a recorded overflow spill) to raise the share of exceedance samples;
- a target of 115 paired samples per estuary, at least 40 of them exceedances, giving an expected half-width of about 0.13 for the 95% CI of sensitivity;
- exchange of 10% of samples as split samples between the CICS and URC culture laboratories;
- a transfer rule (section 7): coefficients from one estuary are accepted for the other only if, in the receiving estuary, the lower 95% bound for sensitivity is at least 0.60 and specificity is at least 0.80; otherwise that estuary keeps site-specific coefficients and the transfer is reported as failed.

Funding for the full campaign has not been secured. Apart from the pilot below, no sampling under the protocol has started.

**Charente pilot.** URC collected 6 paired samples at three stations at the mouth of the Charente between 22 July and 28 August 2026 (salinity 12–31). By culture, 1 sample exceeded 500 MPN/100 mL. The classifier with BAYPROXY coefficients flagged that sample and gave one false positive; 5 of 6 samples were classified correctly. With one exceedance, these data give no usable estimate of sensitivity or specificity in the Charente. The only sensitivity estimate remains the Corrib value of 0.76 (bootstrap 95% CI 0.55–0.90), which is preliminary. Cross-estuary validation has not been done.

**Shannon Estuary Laboratory.** The CICS Shannon Estuary Laboratory ran the proxy assay on 20 split samples from Galway in April–May 2026; its exceedance classification agreed with the Galway laboratory in 18 of 20 samples. No samples from the Shannon estuary have been collected.

## 2. Decision-cost table (ESR, Excellence, second shortcoming)

WISW drafted a decision-cost table (draft v0.2, 31 July 2026; authors J. Kettler and H. Wolfsteller) to replace the fixed 0.5 warning probability with a cost-based rule. Costs are per beach-day and bathing water.

| Outcome | Bears the cost | Cost items | Range (EUR) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Warning, exceedance occurs | Local authority; bathers | Signage and staff (avoided illness not counted) | 1,900–4,600 |
| Warning, no exceedance (false alarm) | Local authority; local businesses | Signage and staff; lost trade; loss of trust (not priced) | 1,900–4,600 |
| No warning, exceedance (miss) | Bathers; health system; local authority | Gastrointestinal illness at assumed attack rates; lost workdays; complaint handling | 14,000–38,000 |
| No warning, no exceedance | none | none | 0 |

Under a cost–loss rule (warn when the predicted probability exceeds the ratio of action cost to avoidable loss), the table implies thresholds between 0.05 and 0.33, with a central value of 0.14 (EUR 3,000 / EUR 22,000), against the fixed 0.5 of the 2025 application. # Final report: BAYPROXY (2021–2024)

**Rapid faecal-contamination proxies and overflow-driven exceedance forecasting for Galway Bay bathing waters**

Funded by the EPA Research Programme 2021–2030, grant 2021-W-MS-47, EUR 398,000, 1 April 2021 to 30 September 2024 (including a six-month no-cost extension). Lead organisation: Cladach Institute for Coastal Science (CICS), Galway. Principal investigator: Dr Sorcha Mulqueeney. Report submitted 20 December 2024.

## 1. Objectives

1. Calibrate a rapid proxy for faecal contamination, combining tryptophan-like fluorescence (TLF) and β-D-glucuronidase (GLUC) activity, against culture-based *E. coli* in the Corrib estuary and inner Galway Bay.
2. Relate storm-overflow spills, rainfall and tide to exceedances at four designated bathing waters (B1–B4).
3. Describe how beach users receive water-quality information.

## 2. Methods

- **Sampling.** Nine stations from the lower Corrib estuary to B1–B4 in the 2021, 2022 and 2023 bathing seasons (1 June to 15 September): routine fortnightly sampling plus event sampling within 48 h of rainfall above 8 mm in 24 h. 142 paired samples (proxy and culture from the same bottle); salinity 4–34.
- **Reference method.** *E. coli* by ISO 9308-3 (miniaturised MPN) in the CICS microbiology laboratory, accredited to ISO/IEC 17025 for this method. Exceedance: a single sample above 500 MPN/100 mL.
- **Proxy.** TLF (peak T) read with a field fluorometer; GLUC activity from a 2-hour fluorogenic assay. A logistic classifier on TLF, GLUC and salinity was fitted with leave-one-season-out cross-validation; the cut-off maximised the Youden index. Uncertainty from 2,000 bootstrap resamples stratified by season.
- **Overflows and forecast model.** Spill telemetry for four storm overflows (2019–2023, 187 spill events) supplied by the national water utility under a data-sharing agreement that prohibits redistribution. Hourly rainfall from Met Éireann gauges. A TELEMAC-2D model of inner Galway Bay (unstructured mesh, 40–250 m) gave outfall-to-beach travel times by particle tracking. A logistic model of exceedance at B1–B4 used 24-h rainfall, spill duration, tidal state and onshore wind, and was evaluated against regulatory and investigative samples from 2019–2023 (486 sample-days).
- **Survey.** Intercept survey of 612 beach users at B1–B4, July–August 2023, in English only.

## 3. Results

- **Exceedances.** 25 of 142 paired samples (17.6%) exceeded 500 MPN/100 mL; 21 of the 25 were event samples.
- **Proxy performance.** Sensitivity **0.76** (19 of 25; bootstrap 95% CI 0.55–0.90); specificity **0.88** (103 of 117; 95% CI 0.81–0.93). Log proxy score correlated with log *E. coli* (r = 0.71, n = 142). Four of the six false negatives occurred at salinity above 30, where the GLUC signal is diluted.
- **Travel time.** Median outfall-to-beach travel time 6.5 h (interquartile range 3.5–11.0 h).
- **Forecast skill.** Area under the ROC curve **0.81** (95% CI 0.74–0.87) over 486 sample-days, of which 38 were exceedances. With warnings issued at a predicted probability of 0.5, 20 of the 38 exceedances were warned (hit rate 0.53) and 8 of 28 warnings were false alarms (false alarm ratio 0.29).
- **Beach users.** 23% of respondents (141 of 612) relied only on on-site signs for water-quality information; 31% (190 of 612) swam outside the bathing season, when no regulatory sampling takes place.
- **Data.** The paired proxy–culture dataset (142 samples, with station metadata) was deposited in Zenodo under CC BY 4.0 in October 2024. Spill telemetry and survey microdata were not deposited: the first is covered by the data-sharing agreement, the second by a consent form that allows release of aggregated tables only.

## 4. Limitations

- All calibration samples come from one estuary. Classifier coefficients may depend on salinity regime, organic-matter background and effluent composition; transfer to other estuaries was not tested.
- With 25 exceedances, the sensitivity estimate is imprecise.
- The proxy targets faecal indicator bacteria; no pathogens (for example norovirus) were measured.
- The 0.5 warning cut-off was chosen for illustration; no bathing-water manager was involved in setting it.
- The survey was a convenience sample in English and under-represents non-English speakers and early-morning and winter swimmers.

## 5. Outputs

Two peer-reviewed articles (2023, 2024), one MSc thesis, five conference presentations, the open paired dataset, and an internal forecast prototype run daily at CICS during the 2024 bathing season (not issued to the public).

## 1. Excellence

### 1.1 Objectives

- **O1.** Transfer a rapid faecal-contamination proxy, calibrated in Galway Bay, to a second European estuary and quantify its performance there.
- **O2.** Build a 24–48 h warning chain from rainfall nowcasts and overflow telemetry to bathing sites, with a skill target of AUC ≥ 0.80 at each site.
- **O3.** Define warning thresholds and integrate warnings into municipal stormwater and beach-management planning.
- **O4.** Release open data and replicable tools for other outfall-affected coastal sites.

### 1.2 Starting point: BAYPROXY results

BAYPROXY (EPA Research Programme, 2021–2024) produced 142 paired proxy–culture samples from the Corrib estuary and inner Galway Bay. The combined fluorescence–enzymatic proxy detected exceedance of 500 MPN/100 mL with sensitivity 0.76 (95% CI 0.55–0.90) and specificity 0.88. An exceedance model driven by rainfall and spill telemetry reached AUC 0.81 on 486 sample-days at four bathing waters. Median outfall-to-beach travel time was 6.5 h, which leaves time for same-day warnings. A survey of 612 beach users showed that 23% relied only on on-site signs.

### 1.3 Methodology

**Proxy transfer (WP2, lead URC).** “The classifier coefficients calibrated in BAYPROXY will be applied unchanged at three bathing sites at the mouth of the Charente estuary. URC will collect 30 verification samples in year 2 to confirm performance.” URC characterises the organic-matter background at all Charente stations by EEM fluorescence and PARAFAC and analyses 24 outfall effluent samples to compare source signatures with Galway.

**Warning chain (WP3, lead CICS).** Inputs: 1-km radar rainfall nowcasts licensed from Skerrymet Radar Analytics Ltd; overflow telemetry from the Irish national water utility; overflow logs from the wastewater operator at the Charente mouth. The BAYPROXY exceedance model is refitted with nowcast inputs and combined with TELEMAC-2D travel times for Galway and a new TELEMAC-2D set-up for the Charente mouth (month 12). Output: exceedance probabilities 24 h and 48 h ahead, produced daily at 06:00 for B1–B4 and the three Charente sites and run in shadow mode (not public) during two bathing seasons. “A warning is issued when the predicted probability of exceedance is 0.5 or higher.”

The proposal passed all thresholds. It was ranked below the budget available for the topic and is not proposed for funding.

## Criterion 1: Excellence (score 3.50)

The objectives are clear, pertinent to the topic and include a measurable skill target. The preliminary data from 142 paired samples are credible, and combining fluorescence and enzymatic signals with hydrodynamic travel times is a sound approach that goes beyond current practice for overflow-affected beaches. Chemistry, oceanography and planning are integrated.

The following shortcomings are identified:

- The calibration of the pathogen proxy rests entirely on samples from one estuary (Corrib). The proposal applies the same coefficients unchanged at the Charente sites and plans only 30 verification samples in year 2. Given the known dependence of fluorescence and enzymatic signals on salinity and organic-matter background, transferability is assumed rather than tested, and the verification set is too small to estimate performance with useful precision.
- Warning thresholds are set at a fixed predicted probability of 0.5 without justification. The proposal does not identify who would act on a warning, what action would follow, or how the consequences of false alarms and missed events would determine the threshold. A decision rule for users is lacking.
- Open science practices are described in general terms, although preregistration of the verification analysis is a positive element.

## Criterion 2: Impact (score 3.00)

The pathways to impact are relevant to the implementation of the Bathing Water Directive. Target groups (local authorities, wastewater operators, bathers) are identified, and communication measures are adequate.

The following shortcomings are identified:

- The headline impact of about 3,400 avoided bather exposures per season is given as a single value. It does not account for proxy misclassification, uncertainty in travel times or in beach attendance, and no range is given. The scale and significance of the expected impacts are therefore not credibly substantiated.
- The dissemination plan commits to publishing all project data, including overflow telemetry, radar inputs and survey data, under an open licence, while the same section states that these data are held under data-sharing agreements and commercial licences. The open-data commitment is not credible as written, and the data management approach is insufficiently thought through.
- The replication target of 20 sites by 2030 is not substantiated, and no end-user organisation has committed to the project.

## Criterion 3: Quality and efficiency of the implementation (score 4.00)

The work plan is coherent, with clear lead responsibilities. The partners are complementary, and CICS and URC have collaborated before. Resources are appropriate overall.

The following shortcomings are identified:

- The risk table is thin; there is no mitigation if too few exceedance events occur at the Charente sites.
- The coordinator has limited experience in managing multi-beneficiary EU projects, although the management structure is adequate.

# OUTFALERT consortium: technical update since the evaluation summary report

Prepared by CICS (S. Mulqueeney) for the consortium partners. Version of 30 September 2026. Covers February to September 2026; all work funded from the partners' own resources.

## 1. Second-estuary calibration (ESR, Excellence, first shortcoming)

**Protocol.** OUTFALERT-CAL-2E v1.0 was approved by CICS and URC on 30 June 2026. It replaces the 2025 design (Corrib coefficients applied unchanged in the Charente, plus 30 verification samples) with:

- independent calibration in each estuary (Corrib, Ireland; Charente, France), coefficients fitted separately and then cross-tested (fit in one estuary, test in the other);
- event-triggered sampling (rainfall above 8 mm in 24 h or a recorded overflow spill) to raise the share of exceedance samples;
- a target of 115 paired samples per estuary, at least 40 of them exceedances, giving an expected half-width of about 0.13 for the 95% CI of sensitivity;
- exchange of 10% of samples as split samples between the CICS and URC culture laboratories;
- a transfer rule (section 7): coefficients from one estuary are accepted for the other only if, in the receiving estuary, the lower 95% bound for sensitivity is at least 0.60 and specificity is at least 0.80; otherwise that estuary keeps site-specific coefficients and the transfer is reported as failed.

Funding for the full campaign has not been secured. Apart from the pilot below, no sampling under the protocol has started.

**Charente pilot.** URC collected 6 paired samples at three stations at the mouth of the Charente between 22 July and 28 August 2026 (salinity 12–31). By culture, 1 sample exceeded 500 MPN/100 mL. The classifier with BAYPROXY coefficients flagged that sample and gave one false positive; 5 of 6 samples were classified correctly. With one exceedance, these data give no usable estimate of sensitivity or specificity in the Charente. The only sensitivity estimate remains the Corrib value of 0.76 (bootstrap 95% CI 0.55–0.90), which is preliminary. Cross-estuary validation has not been done.

**Shannon Estuary Laboratory.** The CICS Shannon Estuary Laboratory ran the proxy assay on 20 split samples from Galway in April–May 2026; its exceedance classification agreed with the Galway laboratory in 18 of 20 samples. No samples from the Shannon estuary have been collected.

## 2. Decision-cost table (ESR, Excellence, second shortcoming)

WISW drafted a decision-cost table (draft v0.2, 31 July 2026; authors J. Kettler and H. Wolfsteller) to replace the fixed 0.5 warning probability with a cost-based rule. Costs are per beach-day and bathing water.

| Outcome | Bears the cost | Cost items | Range (EUR) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Warning, exceedance occurs | Local authority; bathers | Signage and staff (avoided illness not counted) | 1,900–4,600 |
| Warning, no exceedance (false alarm) | Local authority; local businesses | Signage and staff; lost trade; loss of trust (not priced) | 1,900–4,600 |
| No warning, exceedance (miss) | Bathers; health system; local authority | Gastrointestinal illness at assumed attack rates; lost workdays; complaint handling | 14,000–38,000 |
| No warning, no exceedance | none | none | 0 |

Under a cost–loss rule (warn when the predicted probability exceeds the ratio of action cost to avoidable loss), the table implies thresholds between 0.05 and 0.33, with a central value of 0.14 (EUR 3,000 / EUR 22,000), against the fixed 0.5 of the 2025 application. Applied to the BAYPROXY hindcast (486 sample-days, 38 exceedances), a threshold of 0.14 would have warned 32 of the 38 exceedances (hit rate 0.84) with 61 warnings in total, 29 of them false alarms (false alarm ratio 0.48).

The table is a draft. Cost ranges come from published illness-cost studies and CICS and URC estimates of signage and staff costs. No local authority, bathing-water manager or wastewater operator has reviewed it; no organisation has agreed to own or apply a decision rule; its usefulness to decision-makers has not been tested. Responsibility for bathing-water management and public information lies with local authorities in Ireland (Bathing Water Quality Regulations 2008) and with the commune in France; in Germany it is set by Land bathing-water ordinances.

## 3. Uncertainty in impact estimates (ESR, Impact, first shortcoming)

The code outfalert-uq v0.3 (Python, 15 June 2026; author Dr R. Tobin-Hayes) propagates, over 10,000 bootstrap replicates: (a) proxy sensitivity and specificity, by resampling the 142 BAYPROXY paired samples; (b) outfall-to-beach travel time, from a 50-member TELEMAC-2D ensemble; (c) beach attendance, from counter data for 2022–2024 with a ±20% recording error.

Re-running the 2025 headline estimate gives avoided bather exposures per season at B1–B4 of median 2,580 (95% interval 1,610–3,390). The 2025 point value of 3,400 assumed a perfectly classifying proxy. The interval covers the Corrib only; transfer uncertainty cannot be included until second-estuary data exist. A manuscript was submitted on 20 August 2026 and is under review. The code is in the CICS internal repository and is not yet public.

## 4. Data inventory (ESR, Impact, second shortcoming)

Data inventory v1.0, 25 September 2026, compiled by R. Tobin-Hayes with partner input, lists 12 data assets: restricted raw (5), shareable derived (5) and already open (2).

review_issues.problem: Fortnightly sampling at nine stations throughout three June–September seasons implies approximately 189–216 routine samples before event sampling. The reported total is only 142, including event samples. No incomplete coverage, exclusions or rotating sampling schedule explains this discrepancy.
review_issues.fix: State the actual station coverage and sampling schedule, and give routine and event sample counts that sum to 142. Explain any missed visits, missing paired measurements or exclusions.

review_issues.problem: The ESR says there is no mitigation for too few Charente exceedance events, but the submitted risk table explicitly mitigates fewer exceedance events through event-triggered sampling. The report does not explain why that mitigation fails to address the Charente case.
review_issues.fix: Revise the criticism to acknowledge event-triggered sampling and identify its specific inadequacy, such as the absence of a contingency when too few events occur despite targeted sampling. Keep the submitted application unchanged.

review_issues.where: technical_update_sept2026.md, section 5, Status by ESR shortcoming
review_issues.problem: The status table covers four of the ESR's eight shortcomings. It does not explicitly explain what changed, or remains unanswered, concerning general open-science methodology, the unsupported replication target and user commitments, the insufficient event contingency, or coordination experience. Statements elsewhere supply some current facts but do not complete the response-to-review record.
review_issues.fix: Add status entries for the remaining four shortcomings, identifying the relevant changes and explicitly recording unresolved points. Do not imply that the data inventory alone resolves the broader open-science criticism.

review_issues.problem: The registry omits several facts essential to an accurate proposal: the E. coli endpoint and 500 MPN/100 mL threshold; absence of pathogen measurements; the individual data-access and redistribution conditions, including the telemetry agreement's expiry; the full transfer-acceptance rule and target of 40 exceedances per estuary; CICS versus URC accreditation; available facilities and data-management effort; and the uncertainty code's non-public status. An aggregate inventory count does not register its constituent restrictions.
review_issues.fix: Add sourced facts for these requirements, limitations and resources, preserving their exact values and conditions. Separate approved protocols and existing capacity from unfunded sampling targets and planned activities.

review_issues.problem: F17 dates both the commitment letters and memorandum to 18 September, although the letters were signed on 9, 11 and 16 September. F11 omits the explicit pilot exception to the statement that protocol sampling has not started. F23 broadens CICS's documented lack of Horizon 2020/Horizon Europe coordination into a lack of any multi-beneficiary EU coordination, which its cited source does not establish.
review_issues.fix: Record the three letter dates separately from the memorandum date; preserve the six-sample pilot exception in F11; and restrict F23 to the documented programmes or add an explicit supporting statement about CICS's wider EU coordination history.

review_issues.where: outfalert_esr_2026.md, Excellence first shortcoming; dossier.yaml, reviewer_criticisms R1
review_issues.problem: Both passages call the assay a pathogen proxy. The assay was calibrated against culture-based E. coli as a faecal indicator, and the final report explicitly states that no pathogens were measured. The terminology incorrectly upgrades what the preliminary evidence establishes.
review_issues.fix: Use 'faecal-contamination proxy' or 'E. coli exceedance proxy' consistently in the ESR and R1, and retain the explicit limitation that pathogen detection or prediction has not been validated.

review_issues.problem: The inventory is described as complete, but none of its 12 assets covers the six raw Charente pilot records or the April–May 2026 Galway–Shannon split-sample results. O1 explicitly contains the historical 142 samples, and D2 contains coefficients and bootstrap outputs rather than these new observations. The new records' sharing conditions are also unspecified.
review_issues.fix: Add inventory entries for the new observations, or explicitly identify a broader asset that contains them. State their holders, access and release conditions, and update the inventory totals and F15 accordingly.

review_issues.where: technical_update_sept2026.md, section 3, Uncertainty in impact estimates
review_issues.problem: The revised result is still labelled 'avoided bather exposures', but the described calculation propagates assay, travel-time and attendance uncertainty without specifying how warnings change bathing behaviour. Attendance is not itself a count of exposed swimmers, and warning delivery, response and the warning threshold affect how many exposures could be prevented. A bootstrap interval does not resolve these missing causal assumptions.
review_issues.fix: Specify the attendance-to-exposure conversion, warning policy, delivery assumptions and assumed behavioural response. Label the result as a conditional modelled estimate, or as potentially avoidable exposures under an explicit response assumption, and state which uncertainties remain excluded.

review_issues.where: bayproxy_final_report.md, forecast methods and results; outfalert_application_2025_abridged.md, section 1.3; technical_update_sept2026.md
review_issues.problem: The evidence does not distinguish retrospective exceedance discrimination from genuine forecast performance. The 486-sample evaluation has no stated training/test separation or information cutoff, while its inputs include observed rainfall and spill duration. The proposed 24–48-hour outputs rely on rainfall nowcasts and telemetry without explaining the day-ahead meteorological forecasts or future spill estimates needed at those lead times.
review_issues.fix: Document how the historical AUC was evaluated, including temporal separation, predictor availability and forecast lead time; label it as retrospective or in-sample if appropriate. # Final report: BAYPROXY (2021–2024)

**Rapid faecal-contamination proxies and overflow-driven exceedance forecasting for Galway Bay bathing waters**

Funded by the EPA Research Programme 2021–2030, grant 2021-W-MS-47, EUR 398,000, 1 April 2021 to 30 September 2024 (including a six-month no-cost extension). Lead organisation: Cladach Institute for Coastal Science (CICS), Galway. Principal investigator: Dr Sorcha Mulqueeney. Report submitted 20 December 2024.

## 1. Objectives

1. Calibrate a rapid proxy for faecal contamination, combining tryptophan-like fluorescence (TLF) and β-D-glucuronidase (GLUC) activity, against culture-based *E. coli* in the Corrib estuary and inner Galway Bay.
2. Relate storm-overflow spills, rainfall and tide to exceedances at four designated bathing waters (B1–B4).
3. Describe how beach users receive water-quality information.

## 2. Methods

- **Stations.** Nine stations from the lower Corrib estuary to the bathing waters: five estuarine and transitional stations (E1–E5) and B1–B4. Sampling in the 2021, 2022 and 2023 bathing seasons (1 June to 15 September).
- **Routine sampling.** 22 fortnightly visits were scheduled (7, 8 and 7 per season) and 21 completed; one visit in July 2022 was cancelled for weather. Each visit covered four of the nine stations on a fixed rotation, so that every station was sampled at least every six weeks: 84 samples.
- **Event sampling.** Within 48 h of rainfall above 8 mm in 24 h, samples were taken at B1–B4 and at the two stations nearest the outfalls (E4, E5): 11 events (3, 4 and 4 per season), 66 samples.
- **Exclusions.** 8 of the 150 samples (3 routine, 5 event) were excluded before analysis: 5 because culture started more than 24 h after collection, 3 because the field fluorometer failed its daily drift check. The analysed set is 142 paired samples (81 routine, 61 event), each with proxy and culture from the same bottle; salinity 4–34.
- **Reference method.** *E. coli* by ISO 9308-3 (miniaturised MPN) in the CICS microbiology laboratory, accredited to ISO/IEC 17025 for this method. Exceedance: a single sample above 500 MPN/100 mL.
- **Proxy.** TLF (peak T) read with a field fluorometer; GLUC activity from a 2-hour fluorogenic assay. A logistic classifier on TLF, GLUC and salinity was fitted with leave-one-season-out cross-validation; the cut-off maximised the Youden index. Sensitivity and specificity are computed from out-of-fold predictions. Uncertainty from 2,000 bootstrap resamples stratified by season.
- **Overflows and exceedance model.** Spill telemetry for four storm overflows (2019–2023, 187 spill events) supplied by the national water utility under a data-sharing agreement that prohibits redistribution. Hourly rainfall from Met Éireann gauges. A TELEMAC-2D model of inner Galway Bay (unstructured mesh, 40–250 m) gave outfall-to-beach travel times by particle tracking. A logistic model of exceedance at B1–B4 used observed 24-h rainfall to 09:00 on the sample day, observed spill duration in the preceding 24 h, tidal state at sampling and onshore wind. It was evaluated against regulatory and investigative samples from 2019–2023 (486 sample-days) by leave-one-year-out cross-validation: probabilities for each year come from a model fitted to the other four years. All predictors are observations available at sampling time, so the evaluation is a retrospective hindcast at zero lead time; no rainfall forecasts were used.
- **Survey.** Intercept survey of 612 beach users at B1–B4, July–August 2023, in English only.

## 3. Results

- **Exceedances.** 25 of 142 paired samples (17.6%) exceeded 500 MPN/100 mL: 21 of the 61 event samples and 4 of the 81 routine samples.
- **Proxy performance.** Sensitivity **0.76** (19 of 25; bootstrap 95% CI 0.55–0.90); specificity **0.88** (103 of 117; 95% CI 0.81–0.93). Log proxy score correlated with log *E. coli* (r = 0.71, n = 142). Four of the six false negatives occurred at salinity above 30, where the GLUC signal is diluted.
- **Travel time.** Median outfall-to-beach travel time 6.5 h (interquartile range 3.5–11.0 h).
- **Hindcast skill.** Out-of-fold area under the ROC curve **0.81** (95% CI 0.74–0.87, bootstrap over sample-days) over 486 sample-days, of which 38 were exceedances. With warnings issued at a predicted probability of 0.5, 20 of the 38 exceedances were warned (hit rate 0.53) and 8 of 28 warnings were false alarms (false alarm ratio 0.29).
- **Beach users.** 23% of respondents (141 of 612) relied only on on-site signs for water-quality information; 31% (190 of 612) swam outside the bathing season, when no regulatory sampling takes place; 57% (349 of 612) had entered the water on the day of interview.
- **Data.** The paired proxy–culture dataset (142 samples, with station metadata) was deposited in Zenodo under CC BY 4.0 in October 2024. Spill telemetry and survey microdata were not deposited: the first is covered by the data-sharing agreement, the second by a consent form that allows release of aggregated tables only.

## 4. Limitations

- All calibration samples come from one estuary. Classifier coefficients may depend on salinity regime, organic-matter background and effluent composition; transfer to other estuaries was not tested.
- With 25 exceedances, the sensitivity estimate is imprecise.
- The proxy targets faecal indicator bacteria; no pathogens (for example norovirus) were measured.
- Skill at forecast lead times was not tested. The AUC refers to a zero-lead hindcast with observed rainfall and observed spills; a day-ahead forecast would depend on rainfall forecasts and predicted spills.
- The 0.5 warning cut-off was chosen for illustration; no bathing-water manager was involved in setting it.
- The survey was a convenience sample in English and under-represents non-English speakers and early-morning and winter swimmers.

## 5. Outputs

Two peer-reviewed articles (2023, 2024), one MSc thesis, five conference presentations, the open paired dataset, and an internal prototype run daily at CICS during the 2024 bathing season that gave same-day exceedance probabilities from observed rainfall and telemetry (not issued to the public; its outputs were not systematically compared with samples).

## Criterion 1: Excellence (score 3.50)

The objectives are clear, pertinent to the topic and include a measurable skill target. The preliminary data from 142 paired samples are credible, and combining fluorescence and enzymatic signals with hydrodynamic travel times is a sound approach that goes beyond current practice for overflow-affected beaches. Chemistry, oceanography and planning are integrated.

The following shortcomings are identified:

- The calibration of the faecal-contamination proxy rests entirely on samples from one estuary (Corrib). The proposal applies the same coefficients unchanged at the Charente sites and plans only 30 verification samples in year 2. Given the known dependence of fluorescence and enzymatic signals on salinity and organic-matter background, transferability is assumed rather than tested, and the verification set is too small to estimate performance with useful precision.
- Warning thresholds are set at a fixed predicted probability of 0.5 without justification. The proposal does not identify who would act on a warning, what action would follow, or how the consequences of false alarms and missed events would determine the threshold. A decision rule for users is lacking.

## Criterion 2: Impact (score 3.00)

The pathways to impact are relevant to the implementation of the Bathing Water Directive. Target groups (local authorities, wastewater operators, bathers) are identified, and communication measures are adequate.

The following shortcomings are identified:

- The headline impact of about 3,400 avoided bather exposures per season is given as a single value. It does not account for proxy misclassification, uncertainty in travel times or in beach attendance, and no range is given. The scale and significance of the expected impacts are therefore not credibly substantiated.

# OUTFALERT consortium: technical update since the evaluation summary report

Prepared by CICS (S. Mulqueeney) for the consortium partners. Version of 30 September 2026. Covers February to September 2026; all work funded from the partners' own resources.

## 1. Second-estuary calibration (ESR, Excellence, first shortcoming)

**Protocol.** OUTFALERT-CAL-2E v1.0 was approved by CICS and URC on 30 June 2026. It replaces the 2025 design (Corrib coefficients applied unchanged in the Charente, plus 30 verification samples in one season) with:

- independent calibration in each estuary (Corrib, Ireland; Charente, France), coefficients fitted separately and then cross-tested (fit in one estuary, test in the other);
- event-triggered sampling after rainfall above 8 mm in 24 h or a recorded overflow spill, spread over two bathing seasons per estuary;
- a target of 115 paired samples per estuary, at least 40 of them exceedances, giving an expected half-width of about 0.13 for the 95% CI of sensitivity. In BAYPROXY, 21 of 61 event samples (34%) exceeded; at that rate about 116 event samples yield 40 exceedances, so the target assumes that almost all samples are taken during events;
- exchange of 10% of samples as split samples between the CICS and URC culture laboratories;
- a transfer rule (protocol section 7): coefficients from one estuary are accepted for the other only if, in the receiving estuary, the lower 95% bound for sensitivity is at least 0.60 and specificity is at least 0.80; otherwise that estuary keeps site-specific coefficients and the transfer is reported as failed.

The protocol has no rule for an estuary that yields fewer than 40 exceedances. Funding for the full campaign has not been secured. Apart from the pilot below, no sampling under the protocol has started.

**Charente pilot.** URC collected 6 paired samples at three stations at the mouth of the Charente between 22 July and 28 August 2026 (salinity 12–31). By culture, 1 sample exceeded 500 MPN/100 mL. The classifier with BAYPROXY coefficients flagged that sample and gave one false positive; 5 of 6 samples were classified correctly. With one exceedance, these data give no usable estimate of sensitivity or specificity in the Charente. The only sensitivity estimate remains the Corrib value of 0.76 (bootstrap 95% CI 0.55–0.90), which is preliminary. Cross-estuary validation has not been done.

**Shannon Estuary Laboratory.** The CICS Shannon Estuary Laboratory ran the proxy assay on 20 split samples from Galway in April–May 2026; its exceedance classification agreed with the Galway laboratory in 18 of 20 samples. No samples from the Shannon estuary have been collected.

## 2. Decision-cost table (ESR, Excellence, second shortcoming)

WISW drafted a decision-cost table (draft v0.2, 31 July 2026; authors J. Kettler and H. Wolfsteller) to replace the fixed 0.5 warning probability with a cost-based rule. Costs are per beach-day and bathing water.

| Outcome | Bears the cost | Cost items | Range (EUR) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Warning, exceedance occurs | Local authority; bathers | Signage and staff (avoided illness not counted) | 1,900–4,600 |
| Warning, no exceedance (false alarm) | Local authority; local businesses | Signage and staff; lost trade; loss of trust (not priced) | 1,900–4,600 |
| No warning, exceedance (miss) | Bathers; health system; local authority | Gastrointestinal illness at assumed attack rates; lost workdays; complaint handling | 14,000–38,000 |
| No warning, no exceedance | none | none | 0 |

Under a cost–loss rule (warn when the predicted probability exceeds the ratio of action cost to avoidable loss), the table implies thresholds between 0.05 and 0.33, with a central value of 0.14 (EUR 3,000 / EUR 22,000), against the fixed 0.5 of the 2025 application. Applied to the out-of-fold BAYPROXY hindcast probabilities (486 sample-days, 38 exceedances), a threshold of 0.14 would have warned 32 of the 38 exceedances (hit rate 0.84) with 61 warnings in total, 29 of them false alarms (false alarm ratio 0.48).

The table is a draft. Cost ranges come from published illness-cost studies and CICS and URC estimates of signage and staff costs. No local authority, bathing-water manager or wastewater operator has reviewed it; no organisation has agreed to own or apply a decision rule; its usefulness to decision-makers has not been tested. Responsibility for bathing-water management and public information lies with local authorities in Ireland (Bathing Water Quality Regulations 2008) and with the commune in France; in Germany it is set by Land bathing-water ordinances.

## 3. Uncertainty in impact estimates (ESR, Impact, first shortcoming)

**Quantity.** The 2025 figure of 3,400 counted, for each 2019–2023 hindcast exceedance day at B1–B4, the mean daily attendance as exposures. It assumed that (i) every attendee enters the water, (ii) a warning issued at a predicted probability of 0.5 or higher, posted on site and online for the whole beach-day, reaches every attendee, (iii) every warned person stays out of the water, and (iv) the proxy classifies perfectly. It is a modelled count of potentially avoidable exposures, not an observed reduction.

**Code.** outfalert-uq v0.3 (Python, 15 June 2026; author Dr R. Tobin-Hayes) removes assumption (iv) and propagates, over 10,000 bootstrap replicates: (a) proxy misclassification, by resampling the 142 BAYPROXY paired samples and reclassifying proxy-flagged exceedance days; (b) outfall-to-beach travel time, from a 50-member TELEMAC-2D ensemble; (c) beach attendance, from counter data for 2022–2024 with a ±20% recording error.

**Results.** Under assumptions (i)–(iii) and the 0.5 threshold: median 2,580 potentially avoidable exposures per season at B1–B4 (95% interval 1,610–3,390), an upper bound. In a sensitivity run that replaces attendance by water entrants (57%, 349 of 612 survey respondents, resampled binomially) and assumes that half of warned bathers stay out of the water (an assumed value; no compliance data exist for Galway Bay): median 740 (95% interval 450–990).

**Not included.** Warning reach and behavioural response (fixed by assumption); error of forecasts at positive lead times (section 5); transfer to other estuaries, which cannot be included until second-estuary data exist; out-of-season swimming; illness given exposure. The intervals cover the Corrib only. A manuscript was submitted on 20 August 2026 and is under review. The code is in the CICS internal repository and is not public.
